title: Don't Come Knocking
full_review:
It just goes to show that a first-rate playwright, a renowned director and a Grade A cast are not necessarily a recipe for success.

"Don't Come Knocking" (Sony Classics) is a mostly unsatisfying film from writer-star Sam Shepard and auteur Wim Wenders, teaming once again, after their 1984 "Paris, Texas," which itself received decidedly mixed reviews.

Their new collaboration tells the story of hard-living actor Howard Spence (Shepard) who, post-meltdown, goes AWOL from his location Western movie set, much to the consternation of the Hollywood studio that, in turn, hires a private eye (Tim Roth) to find him.

After giving his spurs and horse to an old geezer in return for the man's plaid shirt and vest, Howard returns home to his mother (Eva Marie Saint) in Nevada, where he hopes for a respite from a career marred by booze, drugs, women, and scandal, as we note when he flips through his mother's scrapbook filled with tabloid clippings of his tumultuous life.

Mom drops the bombshell that Howard has a grown son in Butte, Mont. Howard travels there and encounters waitress Doreen (Jessica Lange), with whom he was involved years ago.

In the bar where she works, Doreen points to Earl (Gabriel Mann), the scruffy on-stage singer as the putative son. Howard later stealthily trails Earl -- who has a strung-out girlfriend, Amber (Fairuza Balk), in tow -- and when Earl threatens him, Howard blurts out that he's his father.

Earl goes ballistic, portending a rocky road for any tender reconciliation.

Meanwhile, a doe-eyed young woman, carrying her mother's ashes in an urn, seems to have more than a passing interest in both Howard and Earl, for reasons you'll guess before they're actually revealed.

Wenders is an accomplished filmmaker, of course, and he adds his artful cinematic vision to the familiar Shepard territory. There is, for instance, a striking sequence where Howard, after a fractious confrontation with Earl, sits in the road on an abandoned sofa, and as the hours pass, he takes stock of his life. It's a magical moment, in purely filmic terms.

Shepard's themes of myth versus reality of the American West, the pitfalls of fame, the human capacity for violence, broken families, loneliness and loss have frankly been better handled in his stage work.

Overall, there's a stilted, artificial quality to the story, and most of the performances never quite ring true, apart from Saint's welcome maternal turn.

This disjointed, slow-moving film will be best be appreciated by Shepard and Wenders' most ardent fans.

The film contains profanity, rough and crude language, some domestic violence, adult thematic material, brief drug references, a crass gesture, dispersal of cremated remains, and brief nudity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
